title: The Room Where It Happens
author: Shaun
summary: This article by an Australian school leader argues that instructional leadership -- deep knowledge of best practice in teaching and learning -- must be non-optional for school leaders. The author observes a cruel irony at the heart of education: the more expert a practitioner becomes, the more likely they are to be promoted into leadership roles that remove them from the classroom. Leadership silos further compound the problem, as each portfolio holder becomes an island, losing sight of the ways everything in education is interconnected -- student management, pedagogy, inclusion, literacy, numeracy, digital learning, and wellbeing all overlap in a Venn diagram of mutual influence. Using the anecdote of a principal who called 'checking for understanding' 'Shaun's Checks for Understanding,' the author illustrates how even a year of school-wide implementation can pass without the building's top leader developing real knowledge of the practice being implemented. The solution proposed includes professional reading, school research leads, leadership book clubs, and rotating leadership portfolios to prevent single-portfolio expertise without broader system awareness.
points: * The career trajectory in education is backwards: the more impact you could have in front of students, the more likely you are to be sitting in a room of adults discussing budgets -- which means the people best positioned to model best practice are systematically removed from the place where that modeling matters most. * Leadership silos in schools are a structural problem: when student management, instruction, inclusion, literacy, digital learning, and wellbeing are each owned by separate leaders who don't need expertise outside their portfolio, nothing that crosses silo lines -- which is almost everything -- gets an integrated response. * The anecdote of 'Shaun's Checks for Understanding' is the article's sharpest moment: a principal calling a research-backed formative assessment practice by the name of the person who introduced it reveals both that the information was brand new when introduced and that a year of whole-school implementation produced no deepening of leadership understanding at the top. * The shared vision requires instructional depth: a principal who can say all the right words ('short cycle formative assessment', 'full participation', 'non-volunteers') without knowing the devil-in-the-details of how those practices actually work is building a house of cards in a cyclone. * Tom Bennett's recommendation of a 'school research lead' -- a designated leader responsible for disseminating up-to-date, evidence-based practice -- is endorsed as a structural response to the time-pressure problem: leaders drowning in operational workload need someone whose job is to bring the research to them.
quotes: Teaching is such a backwards profession at times. The more of an expert you become, the more you are removed from the classroom. The greater the impact you could have in front of a room of students, the more likely it is you're sitting in a room of adults discussing budgets or policy.

Sure, you might be able to say all of the right words! 'Short cycle formative assessment!', 'full participation', 'non-volunteers', but in the case of leading explicit instruction, the devil is in the details.

After spending some time at a school which is the textbook example of a knowledge rich low-variance curriculum I took what I had learned and tried to apply them in less privileged environments... Almost a year into this implementation the Principal of the school referred to them as 'Shaun's Checks for Understanding'. I love getting credit for a concept that first came into prominence from an educator from UCLI in the 1970s, but calling them Shaun's checks shows a massive issue at the top of the totem pole when it comes to educational leadership.

Nothing in education is in isolation. All of these elements interact and overlap. Yet when every action taken by leadership is sending a message to staff whether intentional or unintentional, these silos can create challenges for culture and change.

Instructional leadership requires principals to free themselves of bureaucratic tasks and focus their efforts on improving teaching and learning. If you're irreplaceable, that's a system failure. Being an instructional leader is not just a responsibility, it is a necessity if a school wants to truly be successful.
